nodes.label: EAD encoding
nodes.one_line: Encode a finding aid in EAD XML that validates against the EAD3 schema and renders in a discovery portal.
know_what: EAD (Encoded Archival Description) — the XML standard for encoding finding aids, maintained by SAA's Technical Subcommittee on Encoded Archival Standards (TS-EAS)
EAD3 — the 2015 revision of the standard: a simplified schema, a separate <control> element for metadata about the finding aid itself, and looser content-model rules than EAD 2002
Document structure — every EAD3 document has two children of the root <ead>: <control> (schema version, maintenance, language) and <archdesc> (the archival description proper)
<archdesc> and levels — the description carries a level attribute (fonds, series, file, item) that must mirror the hierarchy in the finding aid and in DACS
Core elements — <did> (descriptive identification with <unitid>, <unittitle>, <unitdate>, <physdesc>), <scopecontent>, <bioghist>, <controlaccess>
Schema validation — an EAD file must validate against the EAD3 XSD (plus the accompanying Schematron rules for business rules) before ingest; unvalidated XML is not a finding aid

Discovery portal rendering — portals such as ArchivesSpace, Calisphere, and the Iowa Finding Aids portal transform EAD to HTML via XSLT; the encoding must be complete enough that the render is navigable
EAD vs DACS — EAD encodes structure; DACS supplies the content rules for what goes inside each element; the two are a pair, not rivals
Crosswalks — EAD maps to MARC-21 and Dublin Core (the 856/856u and dc:relation links), so one encoded description feeds catalogs and portals alike
Namespaces and well-formedness — an EAD3 document declares the etdlns namespace; well-formedness (parses) and validity (conforms to the XSD) are separate checks that both must pass
know_how: Build an EAD3 file from an empty template: write <control> first (schema version, language, maintenance history), then <archdesc> with <did>, then the narrative and access elements
Validate against the EAD3 XSD with xmllint --schema or oXygen and fix every error — attribute typos, wrong level values, out-of-order elements — until zero errors remain

Encode a DACS-compliant finding aid element by element: DACS scope and content → <scopecontent>, biographical note → <bioghist>, access points → <controlaccess> with source attributes (lcsh, lcgft, viaf)
Round-trip a finding aid through ArchivesSpace's EAD import/export and diff the result to see what the system normalizes
Put authority-controlled headings into <controlaccess> (<persname>, <corpname>, <subject>) with the source attribute, never typing names freehand
Render the encoded file to HTML in a portal and verify every series and file level displays with working links and dates
Write a minimal valid EAD3 document by hand with no generator, then prove it validates — the test that separates encoders from form fillers
habits: Validate before publishing: no EAD file leaves the workstation unvalidated
Keep <control> honest — schema version and maintenance dates belong there, and they go stale fast
Encode at the level the portal displays, not the level the XML makes convenient
Reuse authority headings in <controlaccess> instead of retyping names and subjects
When a portal renders badly, suspect the encoding first, the portal second

know_why.claim: EAD XML is the archival discovery standard because a schema-validated structured encoding lets finding aids interoperate across systems, aggregators, and migrations.
know_why.because: a schema-backed format keeps descriptions machine-actionable — portals render them, aggregators harvest them, crosswalks convert them, and the description survives system migrations that kill hand-rolled HTML.
know_why.disputed_by: the web-native camp of archival web developers and user-centered finding-aid researchers (e.g., Cory Nimer and Jody Perkins, 'Trust Us: A Case Study in Finding Aids, Browsing, and the User', Journal of Western Archives 2013), who argue that plain HTML or markdown pages serve users better, that EAD is a library-world artifact of the SGML era, and that its XML overhead buys interoperation for systems rather than discovery for people.
know_why.source: EAD3: Encoded Archival Description Version 3.0 Technical Specification (SAA TS-EAS, 2015); ArchivesSpace EAD import/export documentation; Nimer & Perkins, 'Trust Us' (2013); xmllint and oXygen validation tooling

nodes.checkpoint: Encode a two-series finding aid from scratch in EAD3 — <control> plus <archdesc> with <did>, <scopecontent>, and <controlaccess> using authority headings — validate it against the EAD3 XSD with zero errors, and render it in a discovery portal where both series display with working links.
nodes.common_failure: Typing XML without validating, so the file fails the schema at ingest and every portal render breaks; or encoding levels that contradict the DACS hierarchy (a file-level title under a fonds-level <c>), which the schema accepts but users experience as a broken tree.
sources: EAD3 Technical Specification, SAA Technical Subcommittee on Encoded Archival Standards (2015)
ArchivesSpace documentation — EAD import and export
Library of Congress, EAD3 schema and documentation (loc.gov/ead)
Cory Nimer and Jody Perkins, 'Trust Us: A Case Study in Finding Aids, Browsing, and the User', Journal of Western Archives (2013)

nodes.label: MARC-21 catalog records
nodes.one_line: Convert a collection description into MARC-21 records that load into OCLC, so archives holdings surface in library catalogs.
know_what: MARC-21 — the Machine-Readable Cataloging format maintained by the Library of Congress; the record format library catalogs and OCLC exchange collections in
Leader and directory — the fixed header every MARC record opens with; the directory maps each variable field's tag to its position, and a broken Leader corrupts the whole record
Variable fields — three-digit tags with indicators and subfields: 245 title, 520 summary/scope note, 545 biographical note, 655 genre headings, 852 holdings location
Collection-level record — one MARC record describing the whole fonds or collection (with 6xx subjects and 655 genres), not item-level entries; item detail lives in the EAD finding aid
OCLC — the cooperative WorldCat catalog where member libraries contribute and reuse records; archives create and export records through OCLC Connexion
856 field — the electronic location field that links the catalog record to the online finding aid, making the brief record the front door to the full description
Encoding level — Leader/17 tells catalogers how complete the record is (blank = full, '4' = core); incomplete fixed fields fail load or downgrade the record
Fixed fields and 008 — the coded positions for date, language, country, and format; errors here are invisible in the display but break sorting and limiting
Authority-controlled access points — 1xx/6xx/7xx headings should match LCNAF or LCSH so the record retrieves with everything else on the same creator or subject
know_how: Convert a DACS-compliant collection description into a collection-level MARC record: 245 title, 520 scope note, 545 biographical note, 6xx subjects, 655 genres
Encode the Leader and 008 fixed fields — type, date, language, country — so the record is complete enough for OCLC load
Create the record in OCLC Connexion, run the format validation, and export it as MARC21 binary or MARCXML
Crosswalk from EAD: <unittitle> → 245, <scopecontent> → 520, <bioghist> → 545, <controlaccess> headings → 6xx/7xx, finding-aid URL → 856
Add the 856 field pointing to the finding aid and verify the URL resolves after the record loads
Match access points against the authority file before saving, so the record merges cleanly with existing headings
Export a batch of records and load them into a test catalog (Koha or an OCLC test record) to prove they load without errors
habits: Start from the DACS description, never from a blank record — the finding aid is the source of truth
Check the Leader and 008 before export; fixed fields are where loads fail
Keep every access point authority-controlled; inventing a heading spelling fragments retrieval
Verify the 856 URL resolves after loading, not months later
Read your record the way a patron does: from the catalog search results page
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a collection-level MARC-21 record from a DACS description — Leader and 008 encoded, 245/520/545/6xx/655 populated, 856 linking the finding aid — load it into OCLC Connexion with zero validation errors, export it as MARC21, and retrieve it by creator in a test catalog.
nodes.common_failure: Treating MARC as a form to fill: copying the title into 245 and skipping the Leader, 008, and authority checking, so the record loads but never surfaces in catalog searches — the archive's holdings stay invisible in the very catalogs the record was meant to reach.
sources: Library of Congress, MARC 21 Format for Bibliographic Data
OCLC, Bibliographic Formats and Standards
SAA, Describing Archives: A Content Standard (DACS)
LC, EAD to MARC crosswalk documentation (loc.gov/ead)

nodes.label: Subject & genre indexing
nodes.one_line: Index a collection with LCSH and form/genre terms, describing what the records are rather than what they mean.
know_what: LCSH (Library of Congress Subject Headings) — the controlled subject vocabulary archivists assign from the official authority file; headings are chosen, never invented

Form/genre terms — LCGFT (Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms) and the Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT) describe what a record IS — correspondence, diaries, ledgers, minutes — as a facet separate from subject
Aboutness vs form — 'what the records are about' (labor unions, a city's history) vs 'what they are' (letters, photographs); archival indexing records both facets
Subdivision order — LCSH's topic—place—time pattern ('Labor unions—United States—History—20th century') that makes a heading precise enough to retrieve
Controlled-vocabulary discipline — one heading per concept, verified against the authority; retrieval depends on consistency, not cleverness
Indexing level — DACS applies subjects and genres at collection and series level, not item by item; item-level subject indexing is a backlog factory
Faceted retrieval — separating the subject facet from the genre facet lets a user filter by either ('Civil War' aboutness and 'letters' form)
Authority lookup — id.loc.gov is the working authority file; every assigned heading must be confirmed there before it lands in a finding aid
Local headings — when LCSH has no fit (community records, local subjects), archives add flagged local headings and reconcile them later

Bias in LCSH — the vocabulary carries the Library of Congress's worldview, including outdated or offensive headings for marginalized groups; Sanford Berman's 'Prejudices and Antipathies' (1971) is the classic critique
know_how: Scan a series container list and produce two separate lists: subjects (aboutness) and genres (form), before opening the first folder
Convert a topic phrase into an LCSH heading with correct subdivision order — topic, then geographic, then chronological
Decide subject vs genre by the test: 'is this what the record is about, or what it is?' — a diary about the war gets both facets
Look up every heading in id.loc.gov before assigning; never type a heading from memory
Apply DACS level rules: assign headings at collection/series level, enough to retrieve the series, not exhaustive enough to catalog every item
Add a local heading with a flag when LCSH fails, and record it in the local authority file for later reconciliation
Reconcile local headings against LCSH on a schedule, merging them once an official heading appears
habits: Ask 'what IS this?' (genre) before 'what is it ABOUT?' (subject)
When stuck for a heading, search the authority file instead of inventing a phrase
Keep the researcher's path in mind: would they search 'letters' or 'Civil War'? — index both
Flag biased or missing LCSH headings rather than silently forcing material into a bad one
Index at the series level and stop — the discipline that keeps backlogs from growing
nodes.checkpoint: Index a five-series collection: assign LCSH subject headings and LCGFT genre/form terms to each series, every heading verified against id.loc.gov with correct subdivision order and the aboutness/form distinction stated per series — a researcher must retrieve each series by both a subject search and a genre search.
nodes.common_failure: Indexing meaning instead of form — assigning 'Vietnam War' as the heading for a box of letters whose honest access points are 'Soldiers—Correspondence' plus a subject for the war — so retrieval depends on the archivist's interpretation of content rather than what the records are. The mirror failure is inventing headings no authority file recognizes, fragmenting retrieval across the catalog.
sources: Library of Congress, Subject Headings Manual (H 1900s series) and id.loc.gov authority files
Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms (LCGFT)
SAA, Describing Archives: A Content Standard (DACS), access-points chapter
Sanford Berman, Prejudices and Antipathies: A Tract on the LC Subject Heads Concerning People (1971)

nodes.label: Metadata standards selection
nodes.one_line: Choose a metadata standard per object type — Dublin Core for digital objects, PREMIS for preservation, EAD for finding aids — and justify the choice.
know_what: Dublin Core — the 15-element vocabulary (DCMES, ISO 15836) for describing digital objects; the lightweight default for digitized surrogates and web resources
PREMIS — the Preservation Metadata: Implementation Strategies data dictionary; its entities (object, event, agent, rights) record what proves a digital object survives
EAD as metadata — the finding aid is itself metadata: hierarchical description of the collection the digital objects belong to
Layer separation — Dublin Core describes the single digital object, EAD describes the collection, PREMIS describes preservation events; conflating layers is the classic selection error
Simple vs qualified Dublin Core — 15 unqualified elements vs dcterms refinements (dcterms:created, dcterms:spatial); qualified DC buys precision at interop cost
Metadata crosswalks — mapping EAD↔MARC or DC↔PREMIS loses detail; choosing a standard is choosing what detail to keep, and every crosswalk should be documented as lossy
Standards vs content standards vs schemas — a vocabulary (DC), a data dictionary (PREMIS), and an XML schema (EAD XSD) answer different questions; 'metadata standard' conflates all three
METS — the structural wrapper (XML) that packages DC and PREMIS around a digital object in one envelope
Fixity and events as metadata — checksums and preservation actions are metadata (PREMIS events), not afterthoughts logged outside the description
Interoperability vs richness — Dublin Core trades precision for interop; PREMIS trades simplicity for provability; the trade is the selection
know_how: Choose a standard per object type in one pass: digital object → Dublin Core; preservation tracking → PREMIS; collection discovery → EAD; structural packaging → METS
Write a qualified DC record for a digitized photograph — title, creator, date, format, identifier (a persistent URL or ARK), rights — with at least 8 of the 15 elements populated
Record a PREMIS event (checksum verification or format migration) with its five required properties: object, event, agent, date/time, outcome
Justify a standard choice in writing against the alternatives — why DC and not MARC for a digital object, why PREMIS and not DC for preservation
Link the object-level DC record to the collection-level EAD description via the identifier element
Package DC plus PREMIS in a METS wrapper for one digital object and verify the XML parses
Read a data dictionary (PREMIS) and locate the semantic unit for a given fact — the skill that makes any new standard self-teachable
habits: Ask 'what am I describing — object, collection, or preservation event?' before choosing a standard
Prefer the standard the community already uses for that object type over the one you know best
Keep identifiers persistent and stated — metadata without stable identifiers is unlinked
Record preservation events in PREMIS terms at the time they happen, not after
When a crosswalk loses a field, note the loss instead of pretending the mapping is lossless
nodes.checkpoint: For a digitized collection, produce a qualified Dublin Core record for one object, a complete PREMIS event for its checksum verification, and a written justification citing why DC (not MARC), PREMIS (not DC), and EAD are the right standards for their layers — the DC record must link to the EAD description via identifier.
nodes.common_failure: Grabbing one standard and applying it everywhere — describing everything in Dublin Core (losing preservation events) or in EAD (overkill for a single object) — because the standard you know beats the standard the material needs. The error surfaces years later as unprovable digital objects and undiscoverable surrogates.
sources: DCMI, Dublin Core Metadata Initiative (dublincore.org)
PREMIS Data Dictionary for Preservation Metadata (Library of Congress)
METS schema and documentation (Library of Congress)
OAIS Reference Model, ISO 14721:2012

nodes.label: Environmental control
nodes.one_line: Specify the archival storage environment — 65°F ±2, 35-45% relative humidity, under 500 lux with no UV — and verify it with a datalogger.
know_what: Temperature spec — 65°F ±2 (18°C ±1) for mixed paper collections per ISO 11799; cooler (50-55°F) for photographic and film material
Relative humidity — 35-45% RH target; RH drives chemical decay and mold far more than temperature, with the danger zones above 65% RH (mold) and below 30% (embrittlement)
Lux — the unit of illuminance; collection areas stay under 500 lux at shelf surfaces, per the ISO 11799 light spec
UV radiation — ultraviolet in daylight and fluorescent tubes accelerates fading and yellowing; UV is filtered at the source (sleeves, window film) and measured with a UV meter
Datalogger — a recording thermo-hygrometer (Onset HOBO, TandD, or similar) that samples temperature and RH continuously; verification means logged evidence, not a spot reading
Fluctuation vs steady state — sudden RH swings do more damage than slow drift; stability beats perfection, and condensation/desiccation cycles are what crack emulsions and cockle paper
HVAC delivery — the archive's climate is delivered by the building's HVAC, not a room unit; portable humidifiers fight the building and mask the real problem
Cold storage — 35-45°F or frozen facilities for nitrate film and color photographs, with their own specs and separate alarms
Microenvironments — boxes and enclosures buffer the room climate; a good box buys days of protection during HVAC failure
ISO 11799 — the standard that specifies document storage requirements: the numbers above, plus building and shelving requirements
know_how: Place dataloggers at shelf height in each room, away from doors, vents, and windows, and log temperature and RH continuously
Set the HVAC target at 65°F ±2 and 35-45% RH, and confirm the building can hold it across a season before writing it into a policy
Download a datalogger (HOBOware or the vendor's software), identify out-of-range periods, and cross-check them against the HVAC log
Filter UV at the source — UV sleeves on fluorescent tubes, film on windows — and confirm with a UV meter reading
Measure light with a lux meter at shelf surfaces and keep collection areas under 500 lux
Respond to an out-of-range reading: find the cause (season, HVAC cycle, water), correct it, and document the event in the climate log
Write a one-page climate report from a year of datalogger data showing seasonal swings and their causes
habits: Trust the datalogger, never the thermostat — the building set point is not the room climate
Review logged data on a schedule (monthly check, seasonal deep dive) instead of after a complaint
When a reading goes out of range, hunt the cause before touching the set point
Keep datalogger records as evidence — they are the proof for the board, the insurer, and the grant
Recalibrate or replace dataloggers per the vendor schedule, typically annually
nodes.checkpoint: Deploy two dataloggers in a storage area, log 30 days of temperature and RH, produce a chart showing the area holds 65°F ±2 and 35-45% RH, and write a one-page report identifying any out-of-range period with its cause — the report must cite the datalogger data, not the thermostat.
nodes.common_failure: Relying on the building's thermostat plus an occasional spot hygrometer reading: 'the room feels fine' substitutes for logged evidence, so seasonal swings and HVAC failures go unnoticed until mold or embrittlement appears — damage that is invisible and permanent. The mirror failure is chasing perfect numbers while ignoring fluctuation, which matters more.
sources: ISO 11799, Information and documentation — Document storage requirements
NEDCC Preservation Leaflets — 'Environmental Control' and 'Temperature, Relative Humidity, Light, and Air Quality'
Image Permanence Institute (IPI), Climate Notebook and environmental guidance
Northeast Document Conservation Center, preservation storage recommendations

nodes.label: Handling & storage
nodes.one_line: Handle and store records safely — nitrile gloves for photographs, supports for bound volumes, upright or flat boxing — so use and storage don't damage them.
know_what: Nitrile gloves — worn for photographs, film, and metal objects; skin oils and salts leave fingerprints that permanently damage emulsions
Glove policy nuance — cotton gloves are out (they snag, shed, and reduce dexterity); clean dry hands are fine for most paper, nitrile for photographs
Book cradles and foam wedges — supports that hold a bound volume open at a safe angle during reading, photocopying, or digitization, protecting the spine and sewing
Upright vs flat storage — bound volumes stand upright, shelved snug so they don't lean; oversized flat items and photographs lie flat in boxes
Flat storage — photographs, maps, and large documents stored flat in archival boxes, interleaved with unbuffered tissue or sleeved so surfaces never touch
Archival enclosures — acid-free folders and boxes (buffered for most paper, unbuffered for photographs) that act as each record's microclimate
Rehousing — moving records into archival folders and boxes in original order, documenting the change; the physical sibling of arrangement
Buffered vs unbuffered — buffered paper has an alkaline reserve (good for acidic paper); unbuffered is required for photographs, where alkalinity attacks emulsions
Handling rules — no pens near records, one item at a time, both covers supported, no elbows on documents, no pulling volumes by the spine top
Box packing — boxes filled snug but never overpacked; oversize and fragile items get flat boxes rather than folders that droop
know_how: Glove up with nitrile for photographs and film, and take the gloves off for paper when they cost dexterity
Open a bound volume on a cradle or foam wedge at a safe angle — never forced flat — for reading, copying, or scanning
Shelve bound volumes upright and snug; lay oversize volumes flat with the spine horizontal, never leaning
House a collection: acid-free folders in acid-free boxes, upright for letter/legal size, flat for oversize, unbuffered enclosures for photographs
Choose buffered vs unbuffered by material: unbuffered for color and black-and-white photographs, buffered acceptable for most paper records
Rehouse in original order, recording what moved where in the processing notes, and never reorder while rehousing
Interleave or sleeve photographs so emulsions do not touch adjacent surfaces
habits: Glove up when the material demands it and glove down when it hurts the work
Never force a volume flat — reach for the cradle
Store by size and format, not by subject: oversize goes flat, bound goes upright
Rehouse in original order and note the change; rehousing is not an excuse to rearrange
When unsure about an enclosure, choose acid-free and unbuffered
nodes.checkpoint: Rehouse a mixed box of letters, photographs, and one bound ledger: nitrile gloves for the photographs, unbuffered sleeves, an acid-free folder per series in original order, the ledger upright and snug on a shelf, and a written rehousing note — a colleague must find any item and confirm no order change.
nodes.common_failure: Handling photographs bare-handed 'just this once' and shelving volumes leaning — each shortcut is individually survivable but compounds into faded edges, broken spines, and fingerprints that no later conservation removes. The other classic: using rehousing as an excuse to reorder, silently destroying original order.
sources: NEDCC Preservation Leaflets — 'Handling Varied Materials' and 'Storage Enclosures for Books and Artifacts'
Library of Congress, Preservation Directorate handling guidance
ALA, An Ounce of Prevention: Integrated Disaster Planning for Archives, Libraries, and Archives (1986)
SAA Dictionary of Archives Terminology — rehousing, buffered paper

nodes.label: Disaster response
nodes.one_line: Run the first 48 hours of a disaster — salvage priorities, freezing wet records, freeze-drying referral — so the collection's loss stays partial.
know_what: The first 48 hours — the window that decides the outcome: stabilize the site, stop the water, prioritize salvage, and freeze what cannot be treated immediately
Mold clock — mold begins on wet paper within 48 hours; the race is to dry or freeze before spores colonize the collection
Salvage priorities — the pre-written list (vital records, irreplaceable originals, high-use series) that tells responders what to save first when everything is wet
Freezing wet records — freezing arrests mold and further damage; wet paper can be frozen and held for months until freeze-drying capacity is available
Freeze-drying — the professional vacuum treatment that removes water without the swelling and distortion of air drying; referred to commercial vendors such as Document Reprocessors or Belfor
Air-dry vs freeze decision — small volumes of plain paper can air-dry with fans and interleaving; coated paper, photographs, film, and large volumes go to freezing
Stabilization — the first tasks: secure the site, stop the water source, stabilize temperature and RH to slow mold, and document damage for insurance
Damage documentation — photographing and logging what is wet, destroyed, or salvageable; recovery funding from insurers and granting agencies depends on it
The disaster plan — the pre-written document (contacts, priorities, vendor contracts, procedures); response is executing the plan, not improvising
Format-specific salvage — wet photographs must stay wet (never dry in contact, emulsions fuse); film and magnetic media have their own first actions
know_how: Run the first 48 hours in order: secure the site, stop the water, stabilize the climate, assemble the response team, and begin salvage by the priority list
Freeze wet records: pack them in plastic crates or bags separated by freezer paper and load them into a commercial blast freezer — or arrange vendor pickup — inside the mold window
Decide air-dry vs freeze per item: small volumes of plain paper → air-dry with fans and interleaving; coated paper, photographs, or large volumes → freeze for freeze-drying
Refer to a commercial freeze-drying vendor with documented volume and formats, and start the container and pickup logistics in the first hours, not days
Document damage before moving anything: photograph each affected area and log every item as wet, destroyed, or salvageable
Stabilize the environment after a flood with fans, dehumidifiers, and lowered temperature to buy time against mold
Test the plan's contact list and vendor numbers once a year — a disaster plan fails at the first expired phone number
habits: Think in hours, not days — mold and cockling are the clock
When in doubt, freeze: freezing rarely hurts paper and always buys time
Salvage by the priority list, never by what is nearest the door
Photograph everything before moving anything — the insurer and the grant both need it
Rehearse the plan annually; a plan never opened is a folder of wishes
nodes.checkpoint: Given a simulated flood affecting 30 boxes (mixed paper, one box of photographs, one set of bound volumes), execute the first-48-hours response on paper: stabilization steps, salvage order from the priority list, a freeze-vs-air-dry decision per format with reasons, the freeze-drying vendor referral, and a damage log with photographs — a reviewer must follow the response start to finish without asking questions.
nodes.common_failure: Starting salvage by grabbing the nearest wet boxes: the wrong material gets air-dried while vital records sit wet, and the response team burns the mold window improvising. The mirror failure is skipping damage documentation, so insurance and recovery funding collapse and the loss is counted twice.
sources: NEDCC Preservation Leaflets — 'Emergency Management' and 'Salvage of Water-Damaged Materials'
Council of State Archivists (CoSA), COSTEP disaster response framework
Getty Conservation Institute, Emergency Response and Salvage guidance
Document Reprocessors and Belfor, commercial freeze-drying and recovery services
